sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Transformers power most modern large language models, with softmax attention serving as their central operation (Vaswani et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2023). Standard attention scores each earlier token by matching its key against the current query, typically incorporating relative positional encodings such as rotary embeddings or distance penalties (Press et al., 2022; Su et al., 2024). Intervening tokens between key and query do not directly enter this score. In many sequences, however, subsequent event renders earlier information obsolete. backspace deletes the last typed character, closing bracket terminates an enclosed scope, and reassignment overwrites variables value. Crucially, such events often invalidate newer key while leaving older keys intact. Several recent mechanisms modulate attention logits via sums, products, or transformations accumulated along the keyquery path (Csordas et al., 2022; Golovneva et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). The Forgetting Transformer (FoX) integrates recurrent forget gates into softmax attention to improve long-context modelling and length extrapolation (Lin et al., 2025a). Selective Attention allows tokens to mark earlier keys as obsolete (Leviathan et al., 2025), and Dynamic Context Pruning (DCP) drops keys to reduce inference memory (Anagnostidis et al., 2023). However, because these mechanisms aggregate path contributions via summation or multiplication, they face two structural limitations. First, token-level forget gates (as in FoX) attenuate keys monotonically with age, which makes it impossible to erase recent token without simultaneously suppressing all older ones. Second, pairwise accumulation (as in Selective Attention and DCP) causes suppression to grow with the number of intervening steps (confounding the depth of an event with its duration) while incurring pairwise computation overhead. We introduce First Passage Attention (FPA), which aggregates the keyquery path by its minimum rather than its sum. Each head computes scalar field at every position and scalar level for every key. keys logit remains unattenuated (the key is alive) as long as the subsequent field stays at or above its level. Otherwise, FPA lowers the logit in proportion to the depth of the deepest dip below that level, regardless of how long that dip lasts. We show that single linear parameterisation encompasses FoX, bottleneck bias, and learned expiry (Sukhbaatar et al., 2021) as special cases. Most notably, when the field and levels share learned walk (a prefix sum of per-token increments), any drop in the walk selectively eliminates only those alive keys whose levels lie above the new value. The alive keys naturally evolve as stack, which allows later token to erase newer key while preserving older ones (Figure 1). We prove that in one layer single constant-dimension FPA head realises every dip-induced alive set, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates need head dimension linear in the number of keys. sections.title: 4.2 Language models
sections.content: We trained four decoders with 12 layers of width 768 and 12 heads of dimension 64 on 2.7B tokens of SlimPajama (Soboleva et al., 2023), following the 125M recipe of FoX (Lin et al., 2025a) with the 32k-token vocabulary of Mistral 7B (Jiang et al., 2023). The models differed only in attention, namely FPA and FoX without positional encoding, Selective Attention with RoPE, and softmax attention with RoPE. We trained all of them with context 2048, one seed and mixed precision (Appendix C). We tested two hypotheses of FPA against FoX, each at level 0.05/7. The first asked whether the test loss of FPA is worse by no more than ln 1.01, that is 1% in perplexity. The second asked whether FPA has lower loss beyond the training length on PG-19 (Rae et al., 2020) or retrieves more passkeys placed beyond it (Mohtashami and Jaggi, 2023). Perplexity and extrapolation. Both tests supported FPA  (Table 2)  . On the SlimPajama test set the loss of FPA was 0.0192 nats below that of FoX, and the upper confidence bound of the difference, 0.0186, lay inside the margin of 0.00995. On 99 PG-19 test books its loss at positions 2048 to 4095 was 0.034 nats lower, with upper bound 0.028. It retrieved all 100 passkeys at lengths 3072 and 4096, against 73 for FoX (p = 7.5 10 9). Longer contexts and other evaluations. In windows of 16,384 tokens FPA and FoX kept flat loss far beyond the training length, while Selective Attention and softmax attention with RoPE did not (Figure 2). sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Path-dependent biases. FoX adds sum of log forget gates (Lin et al., 2025a), and it is the stack form of FPA with walk that never rises. Its bias falls with the age of key, so its visible sets are suffixes. Stick-breaking attention (Tan et al., 2025), the geometric attention of the Neural Data Router (Csordas et al., 2022), contextual position encoding (Golovneva et al., 2024), PaTH (Yang et al., 2025) and GRAPE (Zhang et al., 2026) change logits through products, sums or transformations along the path. GRAPE contains FoX and ALiBi as special cases. Selective Attention (Leviathan et al., 2025) and DCP (Anagnostidis et al., 2023) let later tokens remove key, and in the hard limit they realise the same alive sets as FPA. Their bias accumulates score for every pair of later token and key, whereas the bias of FPA depends only on scalars of single positions and costs less to compute than that of Selective Attention (Section 4.3). The suppression of Selective Attention also adds up over the path, so it depends on the duration of dip (Proposition 3.4), and in both methods one mask serves all heads of layer (Proposition 3.6). The concurrent Universal Attention also accumulates pairwise sum along the path and evicts keys whose bias passes threshold (Wertheimer et al., 2026). Range extremes and stacks. StructFormer compares maximum over range with level through sigmoid, the smooth form of the same comparison (Shen et al., 2021). Its level belongs to the token that attends, however, so fixed token sees contiguous span, and the comparison feeds parser that the whole layer shares in masked language model. PRPN (Shen et al., 2018) and syntax-guided local attention (Hou et al., 2022) also gate by range extreme against threshold of the query, and our variant of FPA with the level of the query learned only suffixes (Appendix B). The strengths of the Neural Stack have the first-passage form as closed form, in an external memory of recurrent network that reads only its top (Grefenstette et al., 2015). Ordered Neurons (Shen et al., 2019b), Ordered Memory (Shen et al., 2019a), Stack Attention (DuSell and Chiang, 2024; Li et al., 2024), Pushdown Layers (Murty et al., 2023), Transformer Grammars (Sartran et al., 2022) and DeltaStack (Nguyen et al., 2026) build stacks or syntax into recurrent or attention models, several with supervision of the structure. FPA learns its walk without such supervision. Expire-Span (Sukhbaatar et al., 2021) and adaptive attention spans (Sukhbaatar et al., 2019) learn when keys expire, which FPA contains as the case of clock as field. Preisach Attention studies extremum stacks as sequence memory, without learned level per key or scores between 9 queries and keys (Frydrych, 2026). Tropical Attention takes max-plus extremes over keys rather than over the path between key and query (Hashemi et al., 2025). Expressivity. Lower bounds on head dimension, rank or precision (Bhojanapalli et al., 2020; Sanford et al., 2023; Amsel et al., 2025; Kozachinskiy et al., 2025; Weller et al., 2026) rest on rank, VapnikChervonenkis (VC) dimension or sign-rank arguments of the kind that Theorem 3.1 uses, and our contribution is the family of alive sets that later dips create. One layer needs linear size for bounded Dyck languages (Bhattamishra et al., 2024), while few layers suffice (Yao et al., 2021; Hayakawa and Sato, 2025), which is why we state the separation for one layer. Soft attention simulates hard attention when its temperature scales with the margin (Yang et al., 2026), as Proposition 3.3 does with its strength. Non-negative gates limit state tracking in linear recurrences (Sarrof et al., 2024; Grazzi et al., 2025), and the walk of FPA may rise as well as fall. Eviction. H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) and attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2024) drop cached keys by heuristics, and adaptive computation pruning skips the blocks that the bias of FoX makes negligible (Lin et al., 2025b). The bias of an FPA key never rises again, so decoder can drop key once its bias falls below threshold, and in the hard limit it drops exactly the dead keys.

sections.title: 6 Limitations and Conclusion
sections.content: Limitations. Our language models had 110M parameters and one seed each, and they trained on 2.7B tokens on one 12 GB partition of Turing GPU, so the comparison may change at larger scale. Conclusion. We have introduced First Passage Attention, which lowers the logit of key by the deepest later dip of learned field below the level of the key. One parameterisation contains the Forgetting Transformer, stack, bottleneck bias and learned expiry. In one layer single FPA head realises alive sets for which positional heads and forget-gate heads with token-level gates need 2 dimensions. Without positional information, no head that subtracts sum of non-negative scores of token pairs fits exactly the targets of dips whose durations vary, while one FPA head does. Preregistered probes agreed with these predictions. 110M-parameter FPA language model was not worse than FoX in perplexity, had lower loss on PG-19 at positions 2048 to 4095 and retrieved every passkey at lengths up to 16,384. Use of large language models. We used large language models to assist with code, literature search, proof checking and editing, and we take full responsibility for the content of the paper.

sections.content: C.1 Models, data and training All four models are pre-norm decoders with RMSNorm, SwiGLU feed-forward network of width 2048, no biases and tied embeddings, with 12 layers of width 768 and 12 heads of dimension 64, following the 125M configuration of FoX (Lin et al., 2025a). Figure 22 and Tables 15 and 16 give the architecture and every setting. The vocabulary of 32,000 tokens gives 109.5M parameters for softmax attention and Selective Attention and 109.9M for FPA. FPA computes its field projection in single precision, uses no positional encoding and learns one strength per head. FoX uses the kernel of its authors without positional encoding and initialises its gate biases at zero, as its paper does for data-dependent gates. Selective Attention uses RoPE, and its selection has the ReLU gradient of its paper. Softmax attention uses RoPE with base 10,000. The training data was chunk of SlimPajama (Soboleva et al., 2023) with every document wrapped in and /s, and the validation and test sets were the first 20M tokens of its validation and test splits. The sources of SlimPajama come with their own terms of use and may include copyrighted text. We cut the training stream into non-overlapping windows of 2049 tokens, visited them in one fixed order for all four models and used each window at most once. Training ran 5,150 steps of 3 after 512 warm-up steps and cosine 524,288 tokens, 2.70B tokens in total, with AdamW (0.9, 0.95), learning rate 2 10 decay to zero, weight decay 0.1 on the matrices, gradient clipping at 1.0 and half-precision autocast with loss scaling. All runs used one 12 GB partition of an NVIDIA Turing GPU (compute capability 7.5, without native bfloat16). Training took 23.8 hours for FPA, 21.5 for FoX, 38.9 for Selective Attention and 26.3 for softmax attention  (Table 15)  . The evaluated model trained with an earlier version of the kernel of Section 4.3, which computes the same function (Appendix E). To time that kernel, we trained second FPA model in an exploratory run of the same configuration with seed 2202, outside the preregistration. Figure 5 shows how the four models trained. FPA started more slowly than FoX and Selective Attention and had higher validation loss at step 250. From step 500 on it had the lowest validation loss of the four at every evaluation. At the end its validation loss lay 0.020 nats below that of FoX, 0.006 below that of Selective Attention and 0.027 below that of softmax attention. C.2 Evaluation and tests The test loss averaged the cross-entropy over the 20M test tokens in windows of 2048. WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017) used its test set, and PG-19 used up to four windows of 4096 tokens per test book and averaged the loss at positions 2048 to 4095 over 99 books. The passkey items hide five-digit number in repeated filler text (Mohtashami and Jaggi, 2023), ten numbers at each of five depths, so 50 items at each of 1024, 2048, 3072 and 4096 tokens. The non-inferiority test resampled documents 10,000 times and compared the upper 1 α quantile of the difference in test loss with ln 1.01. The extrapolation test resampled books and asked for an upper 1 α/2 quantile below zero, and the passkey test was an exact one-sided McNemar test at α/2 on the items at 3072 and 4096. Evaluating in single precision changed the difference of the first test by less than 10 6. C.3 Amendments Three amendments changed the preregistration during the runs, and each was frozen before the result it affects existed. The first round of training, with reference implementation of FPA at context 512, stopped before its first checkpoint, and the round reported here replaced it. The PG-19 evaluation first kept the carriage returns of the books, token that the training data never contained, so we amended the extrapolation test to Unix newlines. We had seen the PG-19 losses of FPA and softmax attention at that point, but FoX, the comparator of the test, had not yet been evaluated. D.1 Architecture All our models are causal decoders with pre-norm blocks, and the methods differ only in the bias that each attention layer adds to its logits  (Table 14)  . Figure 22 shows the FPA model down to the operations of one head. FPA computes its three scalars per head with one linear map from the same normalised input as the queries, keys and values. The walk sums the increments over positions, the range minimum runs over the positions after each key, and the strength turns the depth of the deepest dip into the bias. The bias enters every head of every layer before the softmax, and FPA uses no other positional information. In training the forward pass takes the hard minimum and the backward pass the gradient of soft minimum with τ = 1 (Section 2). Our kernel computes the range minimum in blocks of 64 positions without matrix of size (Appendix E). sections.title: E Kernel and cost
sections.content: Our kernel computes FPA with its straight-through minimum in fused Triton kernels on grid of blocks of 64 positions shared by queries and keys. For query block and an earlier key block the forward pass forms the range minimum from the suffix minima of the key block, the minimum over the blocks in between and the prefix minima of the query block. It runs the longest query blocks first. The backward pass needs the gradient of the soft minimum, whose normaliser has the same three parts. It computes the gradient of the field in four parts, for the positions in the key block, in the query block, in the blocks in between and in the diagonal block. All exponentials are powers of two of quantities in the log-two domain, the key side works on transposed tiles, and no value is added atomically, so the gradients are deterministic. The evaluated FPA language model trained with an earlier version of this kernel. Against reference implementation in double precision, 3 in the gradient of the strength for that version had relative errors of at most 5.1 10 4 in tied values of the field. In exploratory checks the current version had the same largest errors, and at most 6.7 10 backward passes over 4096 and 8192 positions. In 200 exploratory training steps the two versions differed less than one version did under different order of summing its micro-batches. 4 on the GPU, except 3.3 10 The benchmark ran on the GPU of Appendix in half precision, with every method timed in the same process and probe for contention before and after each part. The bias of FoX inside our kernel took 1.05 times as long as the kernel of FoX, so the extra time of FPA in Table 3 comes from the operations that FPA adds. The decoding times of Table 3 hardly changed with the length of the prompt, from 1024 to 16,384 tokens, because fixed costs dominate at batch size 1.
